narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tipri originates from the Patiala and Ambala districts.
It is historically linked to the Bavan Dvadasi festival, which celebrates the victory of Lord Vishnu over Raja Bali.
The dance has been compared to the Dandiya of Gujarat and the Tipni of Rajasthan.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tipri is performed during the Bavan Dvadasi festival, a local event in Patiala and Ambala districts held during the lunar month of Bhadra to celebrate the victory of Lord Vishnu.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a circle or in pairs.
Participants use small sticks to create rhythm by striking them against their own sticks or those of other dancers.
In one version, dancers hold ropes tied to a central pole, weaving them while dancing.
Watch for Rope weaving, Stick striking.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (iBgHjDXDBxs)
Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instruments are small sticks held by the dancers.
In the girls' style of Tipri, there is no singing involved; the rhythm is created solely by tapping the sticks.
Listen for the Small sticks.
The sound is primarily percussive, created by the tapping and striking of small sticks held by the dancers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The dance has variants including the rope-weaving style (Patiala), the girls' stick-tapping style, and the dandaas style (Multan, Bahawalpur, and north-western Punjab).

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Tipri dance (India). Instruments: Small sticks. Vocal style: None (in the girls' style). Mood: rhythmic, festive. It should sound like this: The sound is primarily percussive, created by the tapping and striking of small sticks held by the dancers. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
